reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
setup: Corporate bond price changes (Y) are regressed on Treasury futures price changes (X): slope $1.07$, $R^2 = 0.85$. The regression is then reversed, with X as the dependent variable and Y as the explanatory one. The reciprocal of the original slope is $1/1.07 \approx 0.93$.
ask: The slope of the reversed regression is:

options.label: Equal to 0.93
options.why: Treated the reverse slope as $1/\beta$. That holds only if $R^2 = 1$; here $R^2 = 0.85$ shrinks it.

options.label: Above 0.93
options.why: Would need $R^2 > 1$. The product of the two slopes is $R^2$, which cannot exceed 1, so the reverse slope is at most $1/\beta$.

takeaway: The two regression slopes multiply to $R^2$, so the reverse slope is $R^2/\beta$, below $1/\beta$ unless the fit is perfect.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: The one-year rate is $8.0\%$ today and next year is $11.0\%$ or $5.0\%$ with equal probability, so its average is $8.0\%$. A two-year zero (par USD 1,000) is priced as the expected discounted value under these true probabilities. A flat 8% for both years would give $1000/1.08^2 = \text{USD } 857.34$.
ask: The tree price of the two-year zero is:

options.label: Below USD 857.34
options.why: Assumed the 11% branch hurts more than the 5% branch helps. Discounting is convex: the gain from 5% outweighs the loss from 11%.

options.label: Equal to USD 857.34
options.why: Replaced the rate by its 8% average. Averaging the discount factors is not the same as discounting at the average rate (about USD 0.66 apart here).

takeaway: Bond prices are convex in the rate, so a rate that is equally likely to rise or fall gives a price slightly above the one at the average rate.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: A European call with strike USD 990 expires in six months on a one-year zero (face USD 1,000). At expiry the bond is a six-month zero, and the six-month rate is $2.5\%$ or $1.5\%$ with equal probability. Rates are semiannually compounded.
ask: At expiry, the call finishes in the money in:

options.label: Only the 2.5% state
options.why: Linked the higher rate to the higher bond price. A higher discount rate lowers the price (987.65, below the strike).

options.label: Both states
options.why: Treated the 2.5% state as in the money as well; its bond is worth 987.65, below the 990 strike.

options.label: Neither state
options.why: Overlooked that the 1.5% state prices the bond at 992.56, above the strike.

working.label: Payoffs
working.display: $0$ in the 2.5% state, $2.56$ in the 1.5% state

takeaway: Lower rate, higher bond price: a call on a bond pays off in the low-rate state.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: In a six-month step tree, a one-year zero (face USD 1,000) will be a six-month zero in six months. It is worth USD 978.00 in state A and USD 982.80 in state B. Rates are annualised, semiannually compounded.
ask: The six-month rate in six months is higher in:

options.label: State B (worth 982.80)
options.why: Read the higher price as the higher rate. A bond is cheaper when it is discounted at a higher rate.

options.label: The two states are equal
options.why: The prices differ, so the discount factors and the rates differ. The implied rates are 4.5% and 3.5%.

takeaway: Bond price and rate move opposite ways: the cheaper state has the higher rate.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: Six-month and one-year spot rates are $2.0\%$ and $2.2\%$ (semiannual). In six months the six-month rate is $2.5\%$ or $1.5\%$ (real-world 50% each). A call, expiring in six months, on the then six-month zero (face USD 1,000) has strike 990. Replicate it with the one-year zero and the six-month zero.
ask: The arbitrage price of the call is closest to:

options.label: USD 0.03
options.why: Scale slip (one decimal place lost): the arbitrage price is ten times larger.

options.label: USD 1.27
options.why: Discounted the real-world expected payoff, $0.5 \times 2.56 / 1.01$. Arbitrage pricing uses the replicating cost (risk-neutral weights), not the 50% probabilities.

options.label: USD 510
options.why: Counted only the long position in the one-year zero ($0.521$ units at 978.36) and left out the matching borrowing.

working.label: Bond price in 6m, up and down rate
Cost of the one-year zero leg

takeaway: The replicating portfolio is long a large bond position funded by large borrowing; the call price is the small difference, far below the real-world discounted payoff.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: Six-month and one-year spot rates are $2.0\%$ and $2.2\%$ (semiannual). The six-month rate in six months is $2.5\%$ (up) or $1.5\%$ (down). A one-year zero (face USD 1,000) is worth $\text{USD } 978.36$ today. If both states were equally likely, the zero would be worth about 980.30.
ask: The risk-neutral probability of the up-rate state must be:

options.label: Below 50%
options.why: Weighted the cheaper bond too little. The market price (978.36) is below the 50/50 value (980.30), so the cheaper up-rate state needs more weight.

options.label: Exactly 50%
options.why: A 50/50 weighting gives $0.5(987.65 + 992.56)/1.01 = 980.30$, not the actual price of 978.36.

takeaway: To match a lower market price, the risk-neutral weights lean toward the state where the bond is cheaper (rates up).

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: The six-month rate is $4.00\%$ and the one-year zero (face USD 1,000) trades at USD 960.23. In six months it is worth USD 978.00 (up-rate state) or USD 982.80 (down-rate state). A call on it with strike USD 980 expires then. Discounting the 50/50 real-world expected payoff at 2% gives USD 1.37.

options.label: Above USD 1.37
options.why: Assumed risk-neutral weights favour the paying state. The call pays only in the down-rate state, and its weight falls from 50% to about 30%.

options.label: Equal to USD 1.37
options.why: Priced with the real-world 50% probabilities. Prices must be consistent with the market zero price, which fixes the risk-neutral weights.

working.label: Payoffs
working.display: $0$ in the up state, $2.80$ in the down state

takeaway: The risk-neutral probability of the paying (low-rate) state is below its real-world 50%, so the arbitrage price sits under the real-world discounted payoff.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: An option pays USD 6.10 or nothing in six months. The risk-free rate is $3.0\%$ (semiannual). Discounting at the risk-free rate with real-world probabilities gives USD 3.00, which implies a real-world chance of the payoff of about 50%. The option actually trades at USD 1.80.
ask: The risk-neutral probability of the USD 6.10 payoff is:

options.label: Above the real-world probability
options.why: Read the 1.80 price as a higher probability. A market price below the real-world expected value means the payoff state gets less weight.

options.label: Equal to the real-world probability
options.why: The two would match only if the market price were 3.00. Pricing at 1.80 forces a lower weight.

takeaway: Risk-neutral probability is whatever weight reproduces the market price; a price below the real-world expected value means a lower weight on the payoff.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: Three-step tree, six-month steps, semiannual compounding. Six-month rate: $3.0\%$ at date 0; $3.5\%$ or $2.5\%$ at date 1; $4.0\%$, $3.0\%$ or $2.0\%$ at date 2. Risk-neutral probabilities are 80% up, 20% down at every node. A flat $3.0\%$ rate over three periods would price a 1.5-year zero (face USD 1,000) at $1000/1.015^3 = \text{USD } 956.32$.
ask: The tree price of the zero is:

options.label: Above USD 956.32
options.why: Counted the lower rates only. With 80% on up-moves, expected rates drift above 3.0%, which lowers the price.

options.label: Equal to USD 956.32
options.why: Rates are not flat in the tree, and the 80% up-weight pushes expected rates to about 3.3% and 3.6% on later dates.

takeaway: When the risk-neutral weight leans to up-moves, expected rates rise above the starting rate, so the price falls below the flat-rate price.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: European call, strike USD 100, expiring at T2, on a three-year 7% annual coupon bond (par 100). At T2 the bond is compared ex-coupon, so its price is $107/(1+r)$ for the T2 rate $r$. From the T1 node where the rate is $5\%$, the T2 rate is $8\%$ or $6\%$ with equal probability.
ask: At T2, the call is in the money in:

options.label: Only the 8% node
options.why: Thought a higher rate means a higher bond price. At 8% the bond is worth $107/1.08 = 99.07$, below the strike.

options.label: Both nodes
options.why: At 8% the bond is worth 99.07, which is below 100.

options.label: Neither node
options.why: At 6% the bond is worth $107/1.06 = 100.94$, above the strike.

takeaway: Only the lower-rate node (higher bond price) can finish above the strike of a call on the bond.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: European put, strike USD 101, expiring in two years, on a 7% annual coupon bond; compared ex-coupon so the Year-2 price is $107/(1+r)$. Year-1 rate is $5.99\%$ or $4.44\%$. From $5.99\%$ the Year-2 rate is $8.56\%$ or $6.34\%$; from $4.44\%$ it is $6.34\%$ or $4.70\%$. Year-2 up-probability is $0.60$.
ask: At Year 1, the put is worth more in the node with rate:

options.why: Linked the low rate to a higher put value. A put gains when the bond price falls, which happens when rates are higher.

options.label: The two are equal
options.why: The Year-2 bond prices reachable differ (98.56 and 100.62 versus 100.62 and 102.20), so the payoffs differ.

takeaway: A put on a bond is worth more where rates are higher, because the bond price is lower and closer to or below the strike.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: Recombining binomial rate tree: an up-move adds $+20$ bps and a down-move adds $-10$ bps, each with probability 50%. The date-0 rate is $3.0\%$. State $j$ at a date means $j$ up-moves. Consider date 12, state 5: 5 ups and 7 downs.

options.label: Below 3.0%
options.why: Counted that there are more downs than ups (7 against 5) and ignored the sizes. Each up adds twice what each down takes away.

options.label: Equal to 3.0%
options.why: Assumed the 50% probabilities make ups and downs cancel. The state has fixed move counts and unequal move sizes.

takeaway: Compare move sizes as well as move counts: 5 ups of 20 bps beat 7 downs of 10 bps.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: In a recombining binomial tree each step is an up-move with probability 50%. The rate at date 12 reaches state 5 only by taking exactly 5 up-moves and 7 down-moves in some order. There are $\binom{12}{5} = 792$ such orderings.
ask: The probability of reaching date 12, state 5 is closest to:

options.why: Counted a single path, $0.5^{12} = 1/4096$, and left out the 792 orderings that lead to the same state.
Used $0.5^5$, only the five up-moves, and left out the seven down-moves.
Used the single-step probability $p = 50\%$ as if it were the probability of the whole state.

takeaway: Many paths reach the same state in a recombining tree: multiply the single-path probability by the number of paths.
